title: Report on Studying Abroad at Freiburg University, Germany
paragraphs: For three months, from 4/4 to 6/24, I was allowed to study at Freiburg University in southwestern Germany. The initial reasons I wanted to apply to this study abroad system of Nagoya University were somewhat impure ones: I wanted to live in a European city, wanted to practise English, and wanted to go to various places travelling. However, by talking with other classmates who aimed to study abroad and by actually doing clinical clerkships at the hospital, I came to strongly feel that experiencing a clinical clerkship overseas while still a student would be an irreplaceable experience even when thinking about the future, and that I should definitely go.

For the clerkship, I was allowed to rotate for one month each through three departments: 4w (Neurosurgery), 4w (General Surgery), 4w (Plastic & Hand Surgery). First, in Neurosurgery, communication within the university there had not gone well and it had not been conveyed that I was coming to Neurosurgery, so there was an incident in which I was kept waiting about two hours while explaining by showing the actual emails exchanged, and from the first day I received the baptism of studying abroad and was toughened. Freiburg University's Neurosurgery is housed in the Neurocenter, a ward specialised in neurological diseases, and was a huge department with six dedicated operating rooms and more than 3000 operations a year. The main clerkship schedule was: from 7:30 a.m. a conference on the previous day's operations, then observing surgery and ward work, studying management and tests in the ICU, and at 14:30 a conference on the next day's operations and a case study meeting by junior doctors, after which we were dismissed. Also, fortunately, a sixth-year Neurosurgery doctor from Thailand came to study abroad at the same time as I was rotating, so I often acted together with him. Since he had experience as a neurosurgeon, he taught me the content of the operations carefully, which was very educational. Because Freiburg University's Neurosurgery is famous for epilepsy surgery, many operations for epilepsy and brain tumours were done, and I was able to see various cases from relatively common to rare diseases. For the next month I rotated through General Surgery not at the university hospital but at a community hospital. I had been told that I could not rotate through General Surgery originally, but when I insisted that I wanted to go because it is a department I am interested in, the administrative staff coordinated it. From this too I felt that one must state one's wishes properly. The clerkship at the community hospital had a different atmosphere from the one at the university hospital, and it was truly a clerkship as a member of the team. May is the vacation season in Germany, and because the number of doctors was small, I was allowed to scrub in on two or three operations a day, and I feel my experience level shot up. That such a vacation season exists also seemed typical of Germany, which values private life and time with family. As for the operations, true to Germany with its many meat dishes, gallstone and colorectal cancer operations were common, and probably because there are more obese people than in Japan, hernia operations were also common. In my spare time I was also allowed to observe the emergency outpatient department and learned about physical findings and ultrasound findings.

In the third month I returned to the university hospital and rotated through Plastic & Hand Surgery. At Freiburg University, I was told that the skills required in Plastic Surgery and Hand Surgery are similar, so they form one department. Here I was allowed to experience a wide variety of operations, such as surgery for facial nerve palsy, excision of soft tissue tumours, plastic surgery for skin defects, breast augmentation, cosmetic surgery, carpal tunnel release and fracture surgery. In observing the outpatient clinic, the doctors explained patients carefully using X-ray, CT and MRI images. The plastic surgery clerkship at Nagoya University is by no means long, and I could not say I had understood the department sufficiently, so by rotating for a month like this I was able to get a glimpse of how broad the scope of plastic surgery is. The department also had a branch on the top floor of a hotel near the hospital, where cosmetic surgery was mainly performed on private patients. The professor went there once a week to operate, and I was also allowed to take part in those operations.

My life abroad passed as described above, but overall they were days when I was saved by the kindness of the people around me and learned the importance of acting proactively myself. The doctors, even though busy, listened to my clumsy English questions and answered them carefully. Also, the people in the dormitory and in the town did not push me away because I could not speak German but tried to understand me. I consider myself fortunate to have been able to do my clerkship in such a blessed environment, and I would like to make use of this experience in my future. Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and everyone at the International Collaboration Office, 西尾-san, the academic affairs staff, those concerned who made efforts for this dispatch, and the many people in Freiburg who gave me this valuable opportunity to study abroad. Thank you very much indeed.
